title: Broadcasting runs backwards as a sum
objectives: Sum a gradient over the broadcast axes so that it has the shape of its input.

screens.title: One bias, five rows
screens.prose: A layer adds a bias row $\mathbf{b} = (0.5, -1, 2)$ to each of 5 rows: $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}$, with $\mathbf{X}$ 5 by 3. The incoming gradient $\mathbf{G} = \partial L/\partial \mathbf{Y}$ is shown. Raise $b_2$ by 0.01: every entry in column 2 of $\mathbf{Y}$ rises by 0.01.
screens.question: By how much does $L$ change, to first order?

hints.text: Each of the five entries in column 2 moves $L$ by $0.01 \times G_{i2}$.
Add column 2 of $\mathbf{G}$, then multiply by 0.01.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Every row of column 2 moved, and each moves $L$ by $0.01 \times G_{i2}$.

byKey.one-row: You used row 1 only. $b_2$ was added to all five rows, so all five changes count.
byKey.mean: You averaged the column. Each row’s change adds in full: there is no division by 5.
byKey.gradient: That is the column sum, the gradient. The change is 0.01 times it.

explain.text: Column 2 of $\mathbf{G}$ adds up to 0.2, so the nudge moves $L$ by $0.01 \times 0.2 = 0.002$. The bias was used five times, and the five effects add, as in level 2.

screens.title: Summed down the rows
screens.prose: Step through the columns. Each frame adds one column of $\mathbf{G}$ and writes the sum into the bias cell it belongs to.

frames.caption: Column 1 of $\mathbf{G}$ adds up to 1.2: that is $\partial L/\partial b_1$.
Column 2 of $\mathbf{G}$ adds up to 0.2: that is $\partial L/\partial b_2$.
Column 3 of $\mathbf{G}$ adds up to 0.6: that is $\partial L/\partial b_3$.

screens.question: What is $\partial L/\partial b_3$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Step to the third column and add it.

byKey.one-row: You took row 1 only. All five rows used $b_3$.
byKey.mean: You divided by 5. Paths add; they are not averaged.

explain.text: Every row used the same $b_3$, so its gradient collects $G_{i3}$ from every row: 0.6. The whole bias gradient is $(1.2, 0.2, 0.6)$.

canvas.caption: Column 3 of $\mathbf{G}$ adds up to 0.6: that is $\partial L/\partial b_3$.

screens.title: Broadcasting runs backwards as a sum
screens.prose: Broadcasting copied $\mathbf{b}$ down 5 rows on the way forward. On the way back the copies’ gradients add up: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_j} = \sum_i G_{ij}.$$ The rule: sum the incoming gradient over every axis that was broadcast, so the result has the input’s shape.

state.caption: The bias gradient $\partial L/\partial \mathbf{b}$, column by column.

screens.question: `b` has shape `(3,)` and `G` has shape `(5, 3)`. Which line gives `b`’s gradient?

options.why: That adds across each row and has shape `(5,)`: one number per row, not per bias entry.
Each row’s use counts in full, so the copies add; the mean is 5 times too small.
That keeps row 1 only. All five rows used `b`.

hints.text: That axis is the rows, axis 0.

feedback.correct: `G.sum(axis=0)` adds down the rows, the axis broadcasting created, leaving shape `(3,)`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which axis did broadcasting add?

byKey.b: You summed along the rows. Broadcasting copied `b` down axis 0, so sum over axis 0.

explain.text: Broadcasting stretched `b` along axis 0, so axis 0 is summed away: `G.sum(axis=0)` has shape `(3,)`, the shape of `b`.

screens.title: A column broadcast
screens.prose: The console checks `G.sum(axis=0)` against central differences: they agree. Now add a column $\mathbf{c}$ of shape `(5, 1)` instead: $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{c}$ gives each row its own $c_i$, copied across 3 columns. Take the same $\mathbf{G}$.
screens.question: What is $\partial L/\partial c_2$?

hints.text: $c_2$ sits in row 2 of every column.

feedback.correct: $c_2$ was copied across row 2, so its gradient is row 2 summed: $0.5 + 0.3 - 0.2 = 0.6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which entries of $\mathbf{Y}$ used $c_2$?

byKey.first: You took one entry. $c_2$ was copied into all three columns of row 2.
byKey.mean: You averaged row 2. The three copies add.

explain.text: Now axis 1 was broadcast, so the sum runs across each row: $\partial L/\partial \mathbf{c} = (0.7, 0.6, 0.2, -0.1, 0.6)$, kept as a 5 by 1 column.

screens.title: Keeping the shape
screens.prose: In code, $\mathbf{c}$ has shape `(5, 1)`, and its gradient must have it too. The backward line adds into `c.grad`.
screens.question: Which expression has shape `(5, 1)` and the right values?

options.why: That has shape `(5,)`. Added to a `(5, 1)` array it broadcasts to 5 by 5, a silent bug.
That sums down the columns: shape `(1, 3)`, the gradient of a row bias.
That is one number, the gradient of a single scalar added everywhere.

hints.text: A gradient has its input’s shape.
Which line keeps the summed axis?

feedback.correct: `keepdims=True` leaves the summed axis with length 1, so the result is `(5, 1)`, like `c`.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the shape each expression returns.

byKey.b: You dropped the axis. `(5,)` against `(5, 1)` broadcasts to `(5, 5)`, which is the wrong shape and the wrong numbers.

explain.text: Summing over axis 1 with `keepdims=True` gives `(5, 1)`. Without it the result is `(5,)`, and `(5, 1) + (5,)` broadcasts to 5 by 5.

screens.title: sum() and mean() backwards
screens.prose: A loss is often a reduction. `Y.sum()` adds all 15 entries of a 5 by 3 `Y`, so each entry gets gradient 1: a gradient of ones. Now take $L$ = `Y.mean()`.
screens.question: What is $\partial L/\partial Y_{ij}$ for one entry? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: A mean is a sum divided by a count.

feedback.correct: The mean is the sum over 15, so each entry gets $\tfrac{1}{15} = 0.0667$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. How many entries does the mean divide by?

byKey.sum: That is the gradient of `sum()`. The mean divides by the count.
byKey.rows: You divided by the 5 rows. `mean()` with no axis divides by all 15 entries.
byKey.cols: You divided by the 3 columns. `mean()` with no axis divides by all 15 entries.

explain.text: `Y.mean()` is $\tfrac{1}{15}$ times the sum, so its gradient is ones over 15: 0.0667 in every entry. A mean along one axis divides by that axis’s length instead.

screens.title: A bias that turns into a matrix
screens.prose: Tom’s `+` backward does `other.grad = other.grad + out.grad` with no sum. For $\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}$, `b.grad` starts with shape `(3,)` and `out.grad` is 5 by 3. His step is `b.data = b.data - lr * b.grad`.
screens.question: What happens?

options.text: `b.grad` becomes 5 by 3, and one step makes `b` 5 by 3
NumPy raises a shape error at the addition, so nothing runs
options.why: `(3,) + (5, 3)` broadcasts without complaint. Only an in-place `+=` into a `(3,)` array would refuse.

options.text: Nothing goes wrong: the extra rows are ignored
options.why: Nothing ignores them. The next forward pass adds a 5 by 3 matrix where a row was meant.

options.text: `b.grad` keeps only row 1 of `out.grad` and drops the rest
options.why: No row is picked out. Broadcasting stretches `b.grad` to fit all five rows.

feedback.correct: One gradient per row is the misconception: the bias has 3 numbers, so its gradient must have 3. Unsummed, the error spreads into `b` itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the shape of `(3,) + (5, 3)`.

byKey.b: You expected an error. Broadcasting accepts `(3,) + (5, 3)`, which is why the bug is silent.

explain.text: Broadcasting turns `(3,) + (5, 3)` into a 5 by 3 array, so the gradient takes the wrong shape and the step spreads it into `b`. Summing over axis 0 first, `unbroadcast`, keeps `b` a row of 3.

screens.title: A scalar broadcast
screens.prose: Now one number $s$ is added to every entry: $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} + s$, with $s$ of shape `()`. Every axis was broadcast. Take the same $\mathbf{G}$.

state.caption: $\mathbf{G}$, and the one number $s$ that every entry used.

screens.question: What is $\partial L/\partial s$?

feedback.correct: $s$ was used by all 15 entries, so its gradient is all of $\mathbf{G}$ added: $1.2 + 0.2 + 0.6 = 2.0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Every entry of $\mathbf{Y}$ used $s$.

byKey.one-col: You added column 1 only. $s$ went into every column.
byKey.mean: You divided by 15. The 15 copies add.

explain.text: A scalar is broadcast along both axes, so both are summed: `G.sum()` is 2.0, the column sums $1.2 + 0.2 + 0.6$ added.

screens.title: unbroadcast() in code
screens.prose: Write `unbroadcast(grad, shape)`: sum `grad` down to `shape`. First sum over any leading axes broadcasting added, then over every axis where `shape` has a 1, keeping that axis. `show(a)` (loaded) prints a result’s shape and values.
screens.question: Write `unbroadcast`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests on shape pairs: `(3,)`, `(5, 1)`, `()` and `(1, 3)` from a 5 by 3 array, `(4, 1)` from a 2 by 4 by 3 array, and an unchanged shape. Each result’s shape and values must match exactly.

mutants.symptom: The summed axis is dropped, so a (5, 1) gradient comes back as (5,).

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def unbroadcast(grad, shape):
    shape = tuple(shape)
    extra = grad.ndim - len(shape)
    axes = tuple(i for i, n in enumerate(shape) if n == 1 and grad.shape[i] != 1)
    if axes:
        grad = grad.sum(axis=axes, keepdims=True)
    return grad
mutants.symptom: The leading axes broadcasting added are never summed.
Copies are averaged instead of added.

hints.text: Compare the number of axes first.
Leading extra axes go with one `sum`.
Then sum, with `keepdims=True`, where `shape` has a 1 and `grad` does not.

feedback.correct: Every shape pair comes back with the input’s shape and the summed values.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing shape pair.

explain.text: Leading axes are summed away; axes of length 1 are summed with `keepdims=True`. Every backward rule for a broadcasting operation ends with this call.

screens.title: One fee rate, many trades
screens.prose: A broker charges every trade the same fee rate $f$: costs = $f \times$ notionals, with $f$ broadcast over four trades of £20,000, £35,000, £15,000 and £30,000. The total cost $C$ is the sum.
screens.question: By how many pounds does $C$ rise if $f$ rises by one basis point (0.0001)? Give the answer in pounds.

hints.text: Its gradient adds over all four trades.

feedback.correct: $\partial C/\partial f$ is the sum of the notionals, £100,000, so one basis point adds $0.0001 \times 100{,}000 = £10$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. $f$ was used by every trade.

byKey.average: You used the average trade. The fee hits all four, so the notionals add.
byKey.largest: You used the largest trade only. All four trades pay the fee.

explain.text: $f$ is broadcast across the trades, so its gradient sums over them: $\partial C/\partial f = £100{,}000$. A rise of 0.0001 costs £10 a round of trades.

ideas: A broadcast input is used once per copy, so its gradient adds the copies’ gradients: sum the incoming gradient over every axis that was broadcast.
Keep the input’s shape: a row bias gets `G.sum(axis=0)`, a column gets `G.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)`, a scalar gets `G.sum()`.
`sum()` passes back ones and `mean()` passes back ones over the count; `unbroadcast(grad, shape)` does the summing for every broadcasting operation.

formula.name: Gradient of a broadcast
formula.note: For a bias row added to every row of a batch.

summary.trap: A gradient left with one row per use has the wrong shape, and broadcasting lets the error spread silently.

quiz.prose: A bias $\mathbf{b}$ of shape `(2,)` is added to 3 rows, and $\mathbf{G} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 0.5 & 1 \\ 2 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$.
quiz.question: What is $\partial L/\partial b_2$?

byKey.one-row: You took row 1 only. All three rows used $b_2$.
byKey.mean: You divided by 3. The copies add.

explain.text: $b_2$ was added to all three rows, so $\partial L/\partial b_2 = -2 + 1 + 0.5 = -0.5$.

quiz.prose: `x` has shape `(4, 1)` and `y` has shape `(1, 3)`, so `x + y` is 4 by 3 with incoming gradient `G`.
quiz.question: Which line gives `x`’s gradient?

options.why: Right values, but shape `(4,)`: it broadcasts wrongly against `(4, 1)`.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which axis was `x` copied along?

explain.text: `x` was stretched along axis 1, so its gradient sums axis 1 with `keepdims=True`: `(4, 1)`.
